Wandering Stars
WAHN-dur-ing STARZ
n. phr. (Jude's figure for false teachers who keep no fixed course)
English wandering + stars, rendering Greek asteres planētai, from planētēs, a wanderer — the word behind English planet, and cognate with planē, error or deceit.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

Jude piles up five figures for the false teachers who had crept in among the churches, and the last is this: “Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever.” The Greek is asteres planētai, and the noun is the one from which English takes planet — the wanderers, the lights that do not keep the fixed station of the constellations. The figure is drawn from navigation. A mariner sets his course by stars that hold their place; a star that wanders is not merely unusual, it is useless and worse than useless, because a man who steers by it is lost. That is Jude's charge against the teachers. They have light, or the appearance of it; they are conspicuous; and they cannot be steered by. The preceding figures run in the same direction — clouds that carry no water, trees that bear no fruit, waves that produce nothing but foam — and all four describe things that promise what they do not deliver. The sentence pronounced is darkness: “to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever.” A light that will not hold its place ends in the dark, and the word reserved says the end is already appointed.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Wandering, roving; unsettled; not keeping a fixed course. Wandering stars, Jude 13, the planets, which keep no fixed station; figuratively, teachers who hold no settled doctrine.

Wandering, roving, rambling, unsettled, having no fixed course.

Greek planētēs, a wanderer, whence the English planet.

Cognate with planē, a wandering, hence error, deceit, delusion.

Wandering stars, Jude 13, lights that keep no station and cannot guide.

To whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever, Jude 13.

Key Scripture

Jud 1:13 — "Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever."

Jud 1:12 — "These are spots in your feasts of charity, when they feast with you, feeding themselves without fear: clouds they are without water, carried about of winds; trees whose fruit withereth, without fruit, twice dead, plucked up by the roots;"

Jud 1:4 — "For there are certain men crept in unawares, who were before of old ordained to this condemnation, ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness, and denying the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ."

2Pe 2:17 — "These are wells without water, clouds that are carried with a tempest; to whom the mist of darkness is reserved for ever."

Modern Corruption

Doctrinal restlessness is now praised as humility and growth, so that the very quality Jude names as damning — keeping no fixed station — is presented as the mark of an honest teacher.

expand to see more

The modern inversion is almost exact. To hold a settled confession is called rigidity; to abandon one position after another is called a journey, an evolving faith, a willingness to sit with the questions. Whole ministries are built on the public narration of doctrinal migration, and the migration itself is offered as the credential. Jude's metaphor answers this directly, because it is a metaphor about usefulness. The question is not whether a teacher has light but whether anyone can set a course by him. The deconstruction genre, in which a teacher dismantles the faith he once professed while retaining his platform and his audience, is the wandering star with a following, and the followers are the ones at sea.

Jude's own prescription stands against it in the same letter: contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints, building up yourselves on your most holy faith, keep yourselves in the love of God. The word once in verse three is the hinge; a faith once delivered is a fixed star and not a wandering one. None of this commends mere stubbornness or the refusal to be corrected by Scripture, which is a different fault with a different cure. The principle to recover is that teachers are to be judged by whether they hold the deposit, that constancy in doctrine is a pastoral mercy to the people who must navigate by it, and that Scripture reserves for the man who will not keep his station the blackness of darkness for ever.
